reading.body:
CyrusOne's Sterling campus carries 44 MW of IT capacity across three buildings, and it is one of only 25 Virginia data centers that publish a power figure at all.

The pattern here is disclosure scarcity, not capacity. Virginia has 330 mapped data center locations, and 25 of them disclose megawattage. The state's published total of 1,603 MW is therefore a floor rather than a census. Sterling's 44 MW is 2.7% of that published total and ranks 12th among the 25 that report. A ranking like that measures who publishes, not who consumes.

For AI, the number that matters at a site is power, and 44 MW is mid-sized. Spread across 420,000 square feet of technical space, it works out to roughly 2.6 MW per 10,000 square feet, a moderate density consistent with mixed workloads rather than a campus built around high-density accelerators. The certifications listed, SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FISMA, and TIA-942, describe compliance and resilience posture, not compute.

What the data does not cover is the part that decides whether this site matters for AI scaling. There is no grid interconnection capacity, no power procurement, no expansion plan, no rack count, and no utilization. The suitability score of 70 is built only from published IT capacity and operator type, and it flags announced expansion as missing. So Sterling is a real 44 MW of load in Northern Virginia, and nothing in this data says whether it grows.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
